\chapter{The Clock, Taken Apart}
\label{ch:el-minuto-y-el-cuarto}
\hlchaptermodality{342}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el minuto, el cuarto, en punto, el horario and la madrugada, and say why the minute and the second are two halves of one Latin phrase.}

Complete ES-C342-madrugada: cut an hour into minutes and quarters, give a time on the dot, ask for a timetable, and name the hours before dawn.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el minuto]{el minuto — the minute, the first small cutting of the hour}

\label{lesson:ES-C342-minuto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{behind}, then \emph{inside}. (\emph{Detrás}; \emph{dentro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la hora — the thing this one cuts up.
  \item el reloj — what shows it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mi-NU-to}, the weight on the middle beat. Every vowel is short and clean; the \emph{u} is always \emph{oo}, never the English \emph{yoo}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el minuto} — \textquotedblleft{}the minute.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{minūtus} meant \emph{made small} — the past participle of \textbf{minuere}, \emph{to lessen}. It says nothing about clocks at all.

The clock meaning came from a piece of medieval bookkeeping. When astronomers divided the hour, they called the first cut \textbf{pars minūta prīma}, \emph{the first small part}, and the cut after that \textbf{pars minūta secunda}, \emph{the second small part}. Both names got shortened to their odd halves: the first small part became the \textbf{minute}, and the second small part became the \textbf{second}.

Which means the word you already have for \emph{second} and this new one are two halves of the same phrase, and neither one was ever a time word.

English keeps the smallness plainly. Something \textbf{minor} is smaller. \textbf{Minus} takes away. To \textbf{diminish} is to make less. \textbf{Minuscule} is tiny. And \textbf{minute} spelled exactly the same way, said \emph{my-NEWT}, still means \emph{very small} — the original sense, sitting in plain sight.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The hour, cut into its first small parts.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el minuto}
  \item \emph{un minuto, por favor}
  \item \emph{cinco minutos}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{minūtus} mean? (Made small.) And what was the full name of the minute? (\emph{Pars minūta prīma} — the first small part.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cuarto]{el cuarto — the quarter, and the four you already count}

\label{lesson:ES-C342-cuarto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{inside}, then \emph{the minute}. (\emph{Dentro}; \emph{el minuto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — the number this is built on.
  \item el minuto — the other piece of the hour.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KWAR-to}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{cu-} is \emph{kw}, and \emph{-uar-} glides in one motion. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cuarto} — \textquotedblleft{}the quarter,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}a fourth.\textquotedblright{}

You have counted \textbf{cuatro} for a long time. This is that number turned into an order: Latin \textbf{quattuor}, \emph{four}, gives \textbf{quārtus}, \emph{fourth}, and Spanish wears that down to \textbf{cuarto}.

So \emph{cuatro} and \emph{cuarto} are one letter apart on the page and one step apart in meaning: the count, and the position in the count. Hearing the difference is worth practising, because the two are easy to swap.

English counts the same way. A \textbf{quarter} is a fourth. A \textbf{quart} is a fourth of a gallon. A \textbf{quartet} is four players. And \textbf{quarantine} is \emph{quaranta giorni}, forty days — forty being four tens, the period ships once waited out before landing.

On a clock, \textbf{y cuarto} is \emph{quarter past}: \textbf{la una y cuarto}. Spanish also uses \emph{cuarto} for a room, which is the same idea — a quarter of a house divided into four.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A quarter of the hour, from the four you already had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cuarto}
  \item \emph{un cuarto}
  \item \emph{la una y cuarto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number is \emph{cuarto} built on? (\emph{Cuatro}, four.) And what is \emph{quarantine}, word for word? (Forty days.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el punto]{el punto — the point, from the prick of a needle}

\label{lesson:ES-C342-punto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the minute}, then \emph{the quarter}. (\emph{El minuto}; \emph{el cuarto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la hora — what this pins down exactly.
  \item el cuarto — the last cut of the hour.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PUN-to}, the weight on the first beat. The \emph{n} before \emph{t} stays a clean \emph{n}, and the \emph{u} is \emph{oo}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el punto} — \textquotedblleft{}the point,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the dot.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pungere} meant \emph{to prick, to pierce}. What a prick leaves behind is a \textbf{punctum} — a tiny mark made by something sharp. That is the whole word: a dot is the hole a needle made.

English carries the needle everywhere. A \textbf{point} is the sharp end. A \textbf{puncture} is the hole. \textbf{Punctuation} is the set of dots pricked into a sentence. Something \textbf{pungent} pricks your nose. And to be \textbf{punctual} is to arrive at the exact pricked spot on the dial — not near it, on it.

Spanish says the same thing with \textbf{en punto}: \textbf{la una en punto} is \emph{one o'clock on the dot}, the hand standing exactly on the mark. English chose the identical picture without borrowing the phrase.

A \emph{punto} is also the full stop at the end of a written sentence, for the same reason.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Now an hour can be given exactly.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el punto}
  \item \emph{en punto}
  \item \emph{la una en punto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{pungere} mean? (To prick.) And what does it mean to be \emph{punctual}? (To land on the exact pricked mark.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el horario]{el horario — the timetable, an hour-thing}

\label{lesson:ES-C342-horario}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the quarter}, then \emph{the point, the dot}. (\emph{El cuarto}; \emph{el punto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la hora — the word this is built on.
  \item el reloj — what keeps the hours it lists.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o-RA-rio}, the weight on the second beat. The \emph{h} is silent, always, and \emph{-rio} is one syllable with a quick glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el horario} — \textquotedblleft{}the timetable,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the opening hours.\textquotedblright{}

This is \textbf{hora}, which you have had for a long time, plus the ending \textbf{-ario} — Latin \textbf{-ārium}, which makes \emph{a thing to do with}. So a \emph{horarium} is \emph{an hour-thing}: the sheet that tells you which hours something happens in.

The ending is worth collecting, because it is English \textbf{-ary} and \textbf{-arium} almost every time. A \textbf{library} is a book-thing, from \emph{liber}. An \textbf{aquarium} is a water-thing. A \textbf{granary} is a grain-thing. And a \textbf{horarium} is an hour-thing.

The \emph{hora} half is English \textbf{hour} — the same word, with the \emph{h} gone quiet in both languages and the vowel wandering. It is also the \emph{horo-} of \textbf{horoscope}, which is a \emph{reading of the hour} you were born in, and of \textbf{horology}, the study of clocks.

A \emph{horario} is what you ask for at a station or a shop: \textbf{¿cuál es el horario?}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
From the hour itself to the sheet that lists them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el horario}
  \item \emph{el horario de hoy}
  \item \emph{¿cuál es el horario?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{-ario} ending do? (Makes \emph{a thing to do with}.) And what is a \emph{horoscope}, word for word? (A reading of the hour.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la madrugada]{la madrugada — the small hours, named for ripeness}

\label{lesson:ES-C342-madrugada}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the point, the dot}, then \emph{the timetable}. (\emph{El punto}; \emph{el horario}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mediodía, medianoche — where this stretch begins.
  \item la noche — the stretch it closes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma-dru-GA-da}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{d} between vowels is very soft, close to the \emph{th} of \emph{this}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la madrugada} — the small hours, the stretch between midnight and daybreak.

Spanish has a whole word for a time English can only describe. English says \emph{the small hours} or \emph{the early morning} and needs several words. Spanish says \textbf{la madrugada} and is done.

It comes from the verb \textbf{madrugar}, \emph{to get up very early}, and behind that stands Latin \textbf{mātūrus} — \emph{ripe}. A ripe fruit is one that came to its proper time, and Latin used \emph{maturus} for anything early, timely, ahead of schedule. Somebody who rose in the dark was rising while the day was still ripening.

English kept the fruit. Something \textbf{mature} is ripe, whether it is cheese or judgement. Something \textbf{premature} arrived before it had ripened. And to \textbf{maturate} is to ripen.

So this stretch of the night is not named for its darkness. It is named for being early, and \emph{early} was named for being ripe.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five pieces of the clock: the minute, the quarter, the point, the timetable, and the hours before dawn.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la madrugada}
  \item \emph{a las tres de la madrugada}
  \item \emph{muy de madrugada}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{mātūrus} mean? (Ripe.) And what does \emph{premature} mean, word for word? (Before it has ripened.)
\end{tcolorbox}
